When you call something psychotic, you are saying it relates to, involves, or is caused by a condition called psychosis — a serious state of mind in which a person loses touch with reality.

Think of it this way: most of us, even when extremely upset, confused, or mentally unwell, can still tell the difference between what is real and what is not. A person in a psychotic state cannot do this reliably. Their mind has broken from shared reality in a significant way.
What Exactly Is Psychosis? (You Need This to Understand the Adjective)

Psychosis is not a diagnosis by itself — it is a cluster of symptoms that can appear in several mental health conditions. These symptoms are what make something qualify as "psychotic."

The main symptoms are:

1. Hallucinations
The person perceives something that does not actually exist in the outside world. The most common form is hearing voices — voices that may comment on the person's actions, give commands, or argue with each other. The person is fully convinced these voices are real, external sounds. Visual hallucinations (seeing things that aren't there), and less commonly, sensory hallucinations (feeling things crawling on the skin, smelling things) also occur. Crucially, to the person experiencing them, these feel completely real — indistinguishable from actual perception.

2. Delusions
A delusion is a fixed, false belief that the person holds with absolute certainty, even when presented with clear evidence that it is wrong. What makes a belief a delusion is not simply that it is unusual or mistaken — it is that:

  • It is clearly out of touch with reality.
  • The person cannot be reasoned out of it.
  • It has no basis in their cultural or social context.

Common examples of delusions: believing that strangers on the street are secretly agents spying on you, believing that the news anchor on TV is sending you personal coded messages, believing you are a famous historical figure, or believing that your thoughts are being broadcast out loud for others to hear. These are not metaphors or exaggerations — the person genuinely, unshakeably believes these things are true.

3. Disorganized Thinking
The person's thoughts become fragmented, incoherent, or jump from one unrelated idea to another in ways that don't make logical sense. When they speak, it may be difficult or impossible to follow their train of thought. In severe cases, their speech becomes what's called a "word salad" — words strung together without coherent meaning.

4. Disorganized or Unusual Behavior
The person may act in ways that seem bizarre, unpredictable, or inappropriate to the situation — such as laughing at something tragic, dressing in a highly unusual and contextually strange way, or being unable to carry out basic everyday tasks.

5. Negative Symptoms (less obvious but equally important)
These are the loss of normal functions: loss of emotional expressiveness (the face becomes flat and blank), loss of motivation or drive, social withdrawal, and reduced speech. These are called "negative" not because they are bad (though they are) but because they represent something being taken away from the person's normal functioning.
How "Psychotic" Is Used as an Adjective

The word "psychotic" can describe different things depending on what noun it modifies:

A psychotic person / a psychotic patient — someone who is currently experiencing psychosis or has a condition involving psychosis.

A psychotic episode — a defined period of time during which someone experiences psychotic symptoms. An episode has a beginning and end; it does not have to be permanent.

Psychotic symptoms — the specific symptoms described above (hallucinations, delusions, etc.).

Psychotic disorder — a category of mental health conditions in which psychosis is the primary or defining feature.

Psychotic features — when a condition (like depression or bipolar disorder) includes psychotic symptoms as part of its presentation, those symptoms are called "psychotic features." Example: "major depression with psychotic features" means the person has severe depression and also has delusions or hallucinations.

Several mental health conditions are described as psychotic or can involve psychotic features:

  • Schizophrenia — the most well-known psychotic disorder; involves persistent hallucinations, delusions, and disorganized thinking over an extended period.
  • Schizoaffective disorder — a condition combining features of schizophrenia and a mood disorder (depression or bipolar).
  • Brief psychotic disorder — a sudden but short-lived episode of psychotic symptoms, often triggered by extreme stress.
  • Bipolar disorder with psychotic features — during very severe manic or depressive episodes, a person can develop hallucinations or delusions.
  • Major depressive disorder with psychotic features — a severe form of depression where the person also experiences psychotic symptoms, often delusions consistent with depression (e.g., believing they have committed terrible sins or that they are already dead).
  • Substance-induced psychotic disorder — certain drugs (methamphetamine, cocaine, LSD, cannabis in high doses, alcohol withdrawal) can trigger psychosis.
  • Psychosis due to a medical condition — brain tumors, certain infections, autoimmune conditions, or hormonal disorders can cause psychotic symptoms.

This is very important, because the word is widely misunderstood.

Psychotic ≠ violent or dangerous. This is the biggest misconception. Most people experiencing psychosis are frightened and confused — they are far more likely to be victims of harm than perpetrators. While some specific delusions can very rarely lead to dangerous behavior, the vast majority of psychotic individuals pose no threat to others.

Psychotic ≠ psychopathic. These two words sound similar but refer to completely different things. "Psychopathic" (more precisely: someone with psychopathy or antisocial personality disorder) refers to a person who lacks empathy, manipulates others, and behaves ruthlessly — but who has a clear grip on reality. A psychopath knows full well what is real. A psychotic person, by contrast, has lost their grip on reality, often while being a fundamentally non-manipulative individual.

Psychotic ≠ neurotic. "Neurotic" describes someone who experiences excessive anxiety, worry, or emotional distress — but who is fully aware of what is real. A neurotic person's contact with reality is intact. A psychotic person's is not. These are very different states.

Psychotic ≠ "just being extreme or irrational." In everyday casual speech, people sometimes say things like "my boss is psychotic" to mean "my boss is unreasonably demanding." This is informal slang and is medically inaccurate — it does not mean what the word clinically means. When used in a medical or psychological context, "psychotic" always refers to the specific loss of reality contact described above.

If you ever want to determine whether the word "psychotic" applies to something, ask this one question: Has the person lost contact with shared reality?

If a person is wildly emotional, very irrational, extremely anxious, or even mean and cruel — but they still know what is real and what isn't — the word "psychotic" does not apply to them.

If a person is hearing voices that no one else hears, holding unshakeable beliefs that are clearly false, or genuinely cannot tell what is real — then "psychotic" accurately describes their condition or state.

• "After days without sleep, he developed psychotic symptoms, including hearing voices and believing strangers were following him."
  • "The psychiatrist diagnosed her with a brief psychotic episode triggered by the trauma."
  • "Schizophrenia is a psychotic disorder that typically emerges in early adulthood."
  • "Her depression had become so severe that it now included psychotic features — she was convinced she was dying of a disease that tests showed she didn't have."
  • "The drug triggered a psychotic reaction in him, causing hallucinations that lasted for hours."

Psychotic describes anything relating to a state of mind in which a person has lost contact with reality — most distinctively through hallucinations (perceiving things that aren't there) and delusions (holding unshakeable false beliefs) — and it applies to people, episodes, symptoms, disorders, and conditions in which this loss of reality contact is the defining feature.
